pages.markdown:
# Scoring basics

Welcome to the basics of scoring in golf! Whether you’re a junior picking up a club for the first time or a parent new to the sport, this learning pack will guide you through what you need to know. Golf is a friendly game where players try to get the ball into the hole in as few shots as possible. Every time you hit the ball, it counts as a “stroke”. You keep track of these on a “scorecard”.

Golf might seem complicated at first, but it’s easy to follow once you understand the basics. You don’t need special or expensive equipment—just honesty, encouragement, and a willingness to learn. There are lots of fun ways to play and many competitions specially designed to be friendly for juniors and beginners. 

Parents, you don’t need to be golfers yourselves; your interest and encouragement are what really matter. This course will cover what counts as a stroke, how to record scores, and what to expect at junior competitions. Ready to get started?

pages.markdown:
# Counting strokes

In golf, every time you swing at the ball with the intention to hit it, it counts as a “stroke”. Even if you miss the ball, that swing still counts as one stroke. The main aim is to complete each hole using as few strokes as possible.

After you have finished a hole (got the ball in the hole), you simply count up how many shots you needed. For example, if it took four swings (including putting), your score for that hole is four.

Here’s a tip: be as honest as possible when counting strokes. Everyone, even professionals, sometimes forget to count properly, so it’s good to check with your playing partners. Golf relies on honesty and fair play. 

Parents can help by keeping a quiet tally or asking the junior golfer after each shot, “That’s one, now two…” This builds good habits early on. Remember, having fun and learning are just as important as the score. 

If you’re unsure, just ask a coach or another adult for help – everyone is there to support you.

pages.markdown:
# Using a scorecard

A scorecard is a handy tool for keeping track of your strokes on each hole. Each hole has its own box on the card. After you finish a hole, you write down the number of strokes it took you to get the ball in the hole. If you played hole 1 in 5 strokes, write ‘5’ in the box for hole 1.

There’s usually space on the scorecard for your name and maybe for other players in your group. After all holes are played, you add up your scores for a total. It doesn’t matter if your handwriting isn’t perfect—the main thing is to be clear and honest.

If you’re not sure how to fill out a scorecard, just ask another player, a parent, or your golf coach. They’ll be pleased to help. Some clubs use special scorecards for beginners—these might only have a few holes to play, and that’s absolutely fine.

Remember: the scorecard isn’t about winning or losing—it’s a way to see how you’re improving each time you play.

pages.markdown:
# Junior competitions

Golf clubs often organise special competitions just for juniors. These are friendly, relaxed, and designed to help children enjoy the game and learn at their own pace. Each competition might be different—some are for beginners, while others are for more experienced juniors. There could be prizes or certificates, but the main focus is always on having fun and showing good sportsmanship.

Competitions can be 3, 6, 9, or 18 holes, depending on age and experience. Sometimes, you’ll play in a team; other times, it will be just you. Parents or adult helpers might walk with the groups to offer support and encouragement, not coaching during play. 

Before the competition starts, listen to the organiser for a simple explanation of the rules and what to do. Don’t be nervous—everyone there remembers what it’s like to play in their first competition! Just try your best, count your strokes honestly, and enjoy playing with others.

If you ever need help or feel unsure about anything, just ask—everyone wants you to feel welcome and included.

pages.markdown:
# Stableford scoring

One popular way for juniors to play is the “Stableford” scoring system. With Stableford, you earn points at each hole based on how many strokes you take. The fewer shots you need, the more points you get! If you have a high-scoring hole, you simply move to the next one without feeling down—this helps keep things positive.

Here’s the basic idea:

- You start each hole trying to get the ball in with as few shots as you can.
- After each hole, you check a simple table to see how many points you earned for your score.
- For most junior events, if you take a lot of shots and can't finish the hole, you can pick up your ball and write ‘0’ points. No need to feel bad—everyone has tough holes sometimes!

Stableford is great because it rewards good holes and helps beginners stay cheerful. If you’re not sure how many points you earned, just check with a helper or coach. Soon you’ll get the hang of it!

pages.markdown:
# Quick check

Let’s quickly check what you’ve learned about scoring and competitions in junior golf. These questions are just for practice—have a go, and don’t worry if you’re not sure of every answer!

questions.question: What do you call it each time you hit the ball in golf?
questions.explanation: Each time you hit the ball, whether you make contact or not, it counts as a stroke.

questions.question: What is a scorecard used for?
questions.explanation: A scorecard is for writing down the number of strokes you take on each hole.

questions.question: If you miss the ball when you swing, does it still count as a stroke?
questions.explanation: Every attempt to hit the ball counts as a stroke, even if you miss.

questions.question: In a Stableford scoring game, what should you do if you take lots of shots on one hole?

choices.text: Pick up your ball and move on

questions.explanation: If you can't finish a hole in a reasonable number of shots in Stableford, just pick up the ball, record zero points and move on. This helps everyone enjoy the round.

questions.question: Are parents allowed to play for their children in a competition?

choices.text: No, but they can offer encouragement
Yes, but only if they are good at golf

questions.explanation: Parents cannot play for their children, but positive encouragement is always welcome.
